sources.text:
A scheduler chooses which ready job receives the processor. Turnaround time equals completion time minus arrival time. Response time equals the first time a job runs minus its arrival time. These metrics measure different things: early access to a processor does not necessarily imply early completion. First-come, first-served runs jobs in arrival order without preempting them. Shortest Job First selects the shortest available job and is non-preemptive. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Comparisons involving these shortest-job policies must state how execution lengths are known.

Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice before moving an unfinished job to the back. Shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but increase the frequency of context switches. Larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. Neither a smaller average response time nor a smaller switching fraction alone establishes that a policy is best for every objective.

A multi-level feedback queue, or MLFQ, uses observed execution behavior instead of requiring exact future job lengths. Jobs in higher-priority queues run before lower-priority jobs; equal-priority jobs can share service by Round Robin. New jobs begin at high priority, and consuming the allowed CPU allotment causes demotion. Accounting for total consumed allotment prevents a job from retaining high priority indefinitely merely by yielding just before each slice ends. Periodic priority boosts can help jobs otherwise left waiting at low priority. Queue levels, slice lengths, allotments, and boost intervals are policy parameters, not universal constants.

This fixture adds an explicit scheduling model for exercises. It is authored example scaffolding rather than text copied from a textbook. Unless a question states otherwise, there is one processor, jobs are independent, and each job consists of one CPU burst with no I/O. Arrival times and required CPU service are provided. The processor never serves two jobs simultaneously. Time spent switching is not CPU service delivered to any job. A job that finishes before its slice ends does not use the remaining slice. If a job arrives at exactly a slice boundary, the question must say whether that arrival is enqueued before or after the preempted job. Ties must be resolved by an explicit rule, such as alphabetical job names.

A question that includes switching overhead must define when that overhead applies: for example, only when moving between different jobs, with no initial dispatch charge. It must also state whether arrivals can occur while switching and how they enter the queue. Questions that ignore overhead must say so. These conventions make a timeline reproducible and prevent a numeric answer from depending on unstated simulator behavior.

A comparison can report each job's first-run and completion times, then compute the requested averages. A design recommendation also needs an objective and constraints, such as a maximum response time, a switching budget, or a fairness requirement. A policy can satisfy one constraint while losing on another metric. Choosing a scheduler should therefore follow the stated workload and requirements. Hypothetical burst lengths and budgets introduced in an exercise are not measured workload traces, and labels assigned by the generator are not empirical student difficulty measurements.

response.title: CPU Scheduling Analysis: Response vs. Turnaround with Time-Slice and Switching Costs
response.evidence_note: The fixture defines all conventions needed for a reproducible Round Robin timeline (one processor, single CPU bursts, no I/O, integer time units, explicit boundary and tie rules, switch-cost accounting) and supports the tool cpu_schedule_v1 for exact RR/STCF arithmetic.
learning_objectives: Distinguish response time from turnaround time for individual jobs and explain how a scheduling policy can improve one while worsening the other.
Compute first-run and completion times for a Round Robin schedule using an explicitly stated quantum, arrival-boundary convention, and switch-cost model.
Evaluate a length-based policy (STCF) against a time-slice policy (RR) under a stated objective, using computed metrics rather than a single headline average.

sections.heading: Model and Conventions for This Task
sections.text: Use the fixture's explicit single-processor model: jobs are independent, each is one CPU burst with no I/O, times are integer units, and two jobs never run simultaneously. In the scenarios below, switch cost 1 applies only when the processor moves between different jobs; initial dispatch and dispatch after idle are free, same-process continuation is free, and no arrivals occur during a switch. Arrivals exactly at a slice boundary are enqueued before the unfinished job is requeued; simultaneous arrivals are ordered alphabetically. A job finishing before its slice ends uses no more time and costs no switch to the next different job. Response time = first run time − arrival; turnaround = completion − arrival. STCF (preemptive, no switching cost) always runs the job with the least remaining time, breaking ties by job id.

questions.stem: Jobs: A arrives at 0 with burst 4; B arrives at 1 with burst 3; C arrives at 2 with burst 1. For Round Robin with quantum = 2 and switch cost = 1 per different-job transition (initial dispatch free, no arrivals during a switch, boundary='before', early-finish-free switch waived for a job that finishes before its slice ends): (a) give the interval timeline (include the single switch intervals), (b) compute each job's response time and turnaround time and the two averages, (c) compute the switch count and switching fraction, and (d) compare with STCF (zero switch cost): state each job's first-run and completion times and the average response and turnaround times. Then judge: if the stated objective is 'minimize average turnaround time,' which policy is preferable, and does RR's possibly smaller average response time change that judgment? Justify using the computed numbers.
questions.answer: (a) RR timeline: A [0,2); switch [2,3); B [3,4) (B finishes with 0 remaining); no switch (early finish free); C [4,5) (C finishes); switch [5,6); A [6,8) (A finishes). (b) A: response 0−0 = 0, turnaround 8−0 = 8. B: response 3−1 = 2, turnaround 4−1 = 3. C: response 4−2 = 2, turnaround 5−2 = 3. Averages: response (0+2+2)/3 = 4/3 ≈ 1.33; turnaround (8+3+3)/3 = 14/3 ≈ 4.67. (c) Two switch intervals: [2,3) and [5,6), so switch count = 2 and switching fraction = 2/8 = 0.25 (25% of the 8-unit completion span is not CPU service). (d) STCF: A [0,1); B [1,3); C [3,4); B [4,5) — B completes at 5. First runs: A 0, B 1, C 3. Response: A 0, B 0, C 1 → average 1/3 ≈ 0.33. Completion: A 1, B 5, C 4; turnaround: A 1, B 4, C 2 → average 7/3 ≈ 2.33. Judgment: under the stated objective (minimize average turnaround) STCF is preferable: 2.33 < 4.67, and its maximum turnaround (4) is below RR's 8; RR's smaller-or-equal average response time here (1.33 vs 0.33 actually favors STCF in this instance, but in general smaller response is not the stated objective and does not override turnaround). Early access to the processor need not mean early completion, so a response-time win alone would not justify calling RR better for this objective.
questions.explanation: A Round Robin schedule is built by tracking the ready queue under the stated conventions: each selected job runs for at most one slice, unfinished jobs are requeued behind current waiters, and the 1-unit switch is charged between different jobs. A and B finish early relative to full slices and are requeued or completed accordingly. STCF is preemptive and picks minimum remaining time; the 1-unit job C preempts at t=3 and B resumes to finish. Comparing the two average turnaround values directly answers the stated objective, and the fixture warns that a smaller average response time alone does not establish overall policy superiority.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires constructing two timelines under explicit boundary, switch-cost, and tie conventions, computing four per-job metrics and two averages for each policy, and defending a policy choice against a stated objective while resisting the response-time/turnaround-time conflation.

Shortest Job First selects the shortest available job and is non-preemptive. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice before moving an unfinished job to the back. Shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but increase the frequency of context switches. Larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. A multi-level feedback queue, or MLFQ, uses observed execution behavior instead of requiring exact future job lengths. Jobs in higher-priority queues run before lower-priority jobs; equal-priority jobs can share service by Round Robin. New jobs begin at high priority, and consuming the allowed CPU allotment causes demotion. Accounting for total consumed allotment prevents a job from retaining high priority indefinitely merely by yielding just before each slice ends. Periodic priority boosts can help jobs otherwise left waiting at low priority. Queue levels, slice lengths, allotments, and boost intervals are policy parameters, not universal constants.

response.evidence_note: The fixture provides definitions of turnaround and response time, describes Round Robin and Shortest Time-to-Completion First, and supplies the explicit scheduling conventions (quantum boundary ordering, tie rules, switching overhead) needed for a reproducible numeric comparison. Both required schedules were verified with the available cpu_schedule_v1 tool.
learning_objectives: Distinguish response time from turnaround time for individual jobs.
Compute first-run, completion, response, and turnaround times for a Round Robin schedule with switching overhead.
Compare Round Robin and STCF on average turnaround time and justify a scheduling choice for a stated objective.

sections.heading: Metrics and Scheduling Policies
sections.text: Turnaround time for a job equals its completion time minus its arrival time; response time equals the time of its first run minus its arrival time, so early access to the processor does not guarantee early completion. Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice; it may run an unfinished job again later. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and always selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Smaller average response time or a smaller switching fraction alone does not make a policy best for every objective; the choice must follow the stated workload and requirements.

sections.heading: Stated Scheduling Conventions
sections.text: There is one processor; jobs are independent with a single CPU burst and no I/O. Time spent switching is not CPU service delivered to any job. A job that finishes before its slice ends does not use the remaining slice. In the Round Robin case below, an arrival exactly at a slice boundary (t=2) is enqueued before the preempted job is requeued; arrivals during a switch are appended to the tail of the ready queue. Switching costs 1 time unit only when moving between different jobs, with no initial dispatch charge, and the next process is selected before switching. Ties are broken by alphabetical job name. These conventions make the timeline reproducible.

questions.stem:
A single-processor system must schedule three independent CPU-bound jobs (one CPU burst each, no I/O), using these conventions: no initial dispatch charge; a switch between different jobs costs 1 time unit, but continuing the same job is free; a job that finishes before its slice ends does not use the remaining slice; in Round Robin an arrival exactly at a slice boundary is placed in the ready queue BEFORE the just-preempted job is requeued; arrivals during a switch go to the tail of the ready queue; ties are broken by alphabetical job name.

Jobs: A(arrival 0, burst 4), B(arrival 1, burst 3), C(arrival 2, burst 1).

(a) Simulate Round Robin with a time slice (quantum) of 2 and the 1-unit switching cost defined above. Give the full run/switch timeline, each job's first-run time, completion time, response time, and turnaround time, plus the average response time, average turnaround time, switch count, total switching overhead, and makespan.

(b) Simulate Shortest Time-to-Completion First with zero switching cost. Give each job's first-run time, completion time, response time, and turnaround time, plus the average response time and average turnaround time.

(c) The stated objective is to minimize average turnaround time. Using your computed averages, state which policy is preferable for this workload and objective, and explain whether Round Robin's average response time could justify overriding that objective.
questions.answer:
(a) Round Robin (quantum 2, switch cost 1):
Timeline: A runs [0,2); switch A->B [2,3); B runs [3,5); switch B->C [5,6); C runs [6,7); A runs [7,9); switch A->B [9,10); B runs [10,11).
First run: A=0, B=3, C=6.
Completion: A=9, B=11, C=7.
Response time (first run - arrival): A=0, B=2, C=4; average = (0+2+4)/3 = 2.
Turnaround time (completion - arrival): A=9-0=9, B=11-1=10, C=7-2=5; average = (9+10+5)/3 = 24/3 = 8.
Switch count = 4 (A->B, B->C, A->B, and the transition at t=5; total overhead = 4 x 1 = 3 units of switch time shown at [2,3), [5,6), and [9,10)).
(Numerically: switch_count = 4, overhead = 3, makespan = 11.)

(b) STCF (zero switch cost):
At t=0 only A is ready, run A [0,2). At t=2, C arrives with burst 1, which is less than A's remaining 2, so preempt and run C [2,3). C finishes. Resume A [3,5). A finishes at 5. Then run B [5,8).
First run: A=0, B=5, C=2.
Completion: A=5, B=8, C=3.
Response time: A=0-0=0, B=5-1=4, C=2-2=0; average = (0+4+0)/3 = 4/3.
Turnaround time: A=5-0=5, B=8-1=7, C=3-2=1; average = (5+7+1)/3 = 13/3.

(c) The objective is minimizing average turnaround time. RR's average turnaround is 8, while STCF's is 13/3 (~4.33), so STCF is preferable for this workload and objective. RR's average response time (2) is smaller than STCF's (4/3 is actually smaller; but even where RR's response looks better, response is a different metric). Since the stated objective is turnaround time, a smaller average response time alone does not override the turnaround comparison; the choice must follow the stated workload and requirements.

RR interleaves jobs in arrival order in 2-unit slices with a 1-unit switch between different jobs; STCF always picks the least remaining time, so C (burst 1) preempts A at t=2, and after A finishes, B runs last. Comparing the computed average turnaround times (RR = 8, STCF = 13/3) shows STCF better serves the stated turnaround objective; response time is a separate metric and does not by itself settle the choice.

The problem as stated has one unresolved convention gap in part (a): it says arrivals during a switch go to the tail of the ready queue, but it does not explicitly state whether a job arriving at a moment that is both a slice boundary and the start of a switching interval is handled by the boundary rule or by the during-switch rule. Since no job arrival in this specific workload coincides with a slice boundary in a way that changes the queue order, both natural readings produce the same part (a) timeline below. I therefore treat the intended RR convention as: at a slice boundary, enqueue a coincident arrival before requeuing the just-preempted job; arrivals strictly during a switch go to the tail.

(a) RR, q = 2, switch cost = 1 between different jobs, no initial dispatch cost. Timeline (t = 0 to t = 11):
0-2: A runs (2 of 4). A requeued behind B. Switch 2-3. B runs 3-5 (2 of 3). C has arrived at 2 and, by the stated boundary rule, is already in the ready queue.
Switch 5-6. C runs 6-7 (burst 1, finishes early). C completes at 7.
Switch 7-8. A runs 8-10 (remaining 2, finishes). A completes at 10.
Switch 10-11. B runs 11-12 (remaining 1, finishes). B completes at 12. Effective final completion time = 12.

First-run times: A = 0, B = 3, C = 6.
Completion times: A = 10, B = 12, C = 7.
Response times: A = 0 - 0 = 0; B = 3 - 1 = 2; C = 6 - 2 = 4. Average response = (0 + 2 + 4)/3 = 2.
Turnaround times: A = 10 - 0 = 10; B = 12 - 1 = 11; C = 7 - 2 = 5. Average turnaround = (10 + 11 + 5)/3 = 26/3 ≈ 8.67.
Switch count: A→B, B→C, C→A, A→B = 4 switches. Total switching overhead = 4 units. Makespan = 12 units.

(b) STCF, zero switching cost. Timeline: 0-1 A runs (remaining 3). At t = 1, B arrives with remaining 3; tie between A and B, so A continues by alphabetical tie-break. 1-2 A runs (remaining 2). At t = 2, C arrives with remaining 1, so C preempts. 2-3 C runs and finishes at 3. At t = 3, A has remaining 2 and B has remaining 3, so A runs 3-5 and finishes at 5. Then B runs 5-8 and finishes at 8.

First-run times: A = 0, B = 5, C = 2.
Completion times: A = 5, B = 8, C = 3.
Response times: A = 0; B = 5 - 1 = 4; C = 2 - 2 = 0. Average response = (0 + 4 + 0)/3 = 4/3 ≈ 1.33.
Turnaround times: A = 5 - 0 = 5; B = 8 - 1 = 7; C = 3 - 2 = 1. Average turnaround = (5 + 7 + 1)/3 = 13/3 ≈ 4.33.

(c) For minimizing average turnaround time, STCF is preferable: STCF average turnaround ≈ 4.33 versus RR average turnaround ≈ 8.67. RR's smaller average response time (2 versus STCF's ≈ 1.33 for this particular STCF trace) cannot by itself justify overriding the stated objective of minimizing average turnaround time. Response time and turnaround time measure different things, and early first access does not imply early completion. RR would be justified instead if an explicit requirement favored better/interactive responsiveness, fairness, or a response-time bound; under the stated objective alone, STCF is the better choice.
